claims.text: Adjusting elemental composition to increase atomic-size mismatch increases lattice distortion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Increased lattice distortion suppresses atomic diffusion at high temperatures.
Suppressed atomic diffusion enhances structural stability at high temperatures.
Suppressed atomic diffusion enhances chemical stability at high temperatures.
Baseline near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit moderate lattice distortion.
Baseline high-entropy nanoalloys typically undergo diffusion-driven phase evolution at high temperatures.
Elemental ratios can be modified while holding processing conditions and overall phase content constant.
Lattice distortion can be quantified through atomic-size mismatch and associated local strain fields.
Local strain fields created by lattice distortion impede atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic diffusion slows diffusion-mediated phase changes.
Reduced atomic diffusion slows oxidation reactions.
Compositional variation can alter high-temperature chemical ordering or clustering in high-entropy alloys.
Nanoalloys with increased lattice distortion will exhibit delayed phase transformations relative to near-equiatomic baseline compositions.
Nanoalloys with increased lattice distortion will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics than baseline compositions.
Greater high-temperature stability will be reflected in more stable lattice parameters and reduced oxide-layer growth over time.
The proposed trend applies above 800 degrees Celsius.
The prediction is restricted to systems in which compositional changes predominantly alter lattice distortion rather than introduce competing stabilization mechanisms or excessive secondary phases.
The quantitative effect on diffusion and the distortion threshold for stabilization depend on alloy system and processing parameters.
Similar or faster phase-change or oxidation kinetics in the higher-distortion group would falsify the proposed role of lattice distortion as the primary mediator.
